In what year was Empress Elisabeth of Austria born?
Empress Elisabeth of Austria: Elisabeth was born into the Bavarian House of Wittelsbach but enjoyed an informal upbringing before marrying her first cousin, Emperor Franz Joseph I, at 16.
In what year was Ron DeSantis born?
Ron DeSantis: Ronald Dion DeSantis (born September 14, 1978) is an American politician, attorney, and former naval officer serving as the 46th governor of Florida since 2019.
In what year was Edward VIII born?
Edward VIII: Edward was born during the reign of his great-grandmother Queen Victoria as the eldest child of the Duke and Duchess of York, later King George V and Queen Mary.
In what year was Diana, Princess of Wales born?
Diana, Princess of Wales (born Diana Frances Spencer; 1 July 1961 – 31 August 1997), was a member of the British royal family.
In what year did George V die?
George V: From 1877 to 1892, George served in the Royal Navy, until his elder brother's unexpected death in January 1892 put him directly in line for the throne.
In what year did Bernard Tapie die?
Bernard Tapie: Bernard Roger Tapie (French: [bɛʁnaʁ ʁɔʒe tapi]; 26 January 1943 – 3 October 2021) was a French businessman, politician and occasional actor, singer, and TV host.

Government of India: India is a parliamentary republic led by the president of India who, as the ceremonial head of state, holds formal executive power.

Whig Party (United States): Henry Clay. The Whig Party was a political party in the United States that existed from 1833 to 1856.
Taoism: Laozi. Taoism or Daoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasizing harmony with the Tao 道.
In which country did the Battle of Rorke's Drift take place?
Battle of Rorke's Drift: Zulu Kingdom. The Battle of Rorke's Drift, also known as the Defence of Rorke's Drift, was an engagement in the Anglo-Zulu War.
In which country was the Western Chalukya Empire?
Western Chalukya Empire: India. The Western Chalukya Empire ( chə-LOO-kyə) ruled most of the western Deccan, South India, between the 10th and 12th centuries.
Holodomor: Soviet Union. The Holodomor, also known as the Ukrainian famine, was a massive man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine from 1932 to 1933 that killed millions of Ukrainians.
In which country was the Portuguese Empire?
Portuguese Empire: Kingdom of Portugal. The Portuguese Empire, c. 1415 to 1999, was the first and longest lasting of the European colonial empires.
In which country did the Mukden incident take place?
Mukden incident: Republic of China. The Mukden incident was a false flag event staged by Japanese military personnel as a pretext for the 1931 Japanese invasion of Manchuria.
In which country is Union Public Service Commission based?
Union Public Service Commission: India. The agency's charter is granted by Part XIV of the Constitution of India, titled Services Under the Union and the States.
In which country is Loch Ness Monster?
Loch Ness Monster: United Kingdom. It is often described as large, long-necked, and with one or more humps protruding from the water.
In which country did the 2019 El Paso Walmart shooting take place?
2019 El Paso Walmart shooting: United States. On August 3, 2019, a mass shooting occurred at a Walmart store in El Paso, Texas, United States.
In which country was Chera dynasty?
Chera dynasty: India. The Chera country was geographically well placed at the tip of the Indian peninsula to profit from maritime trade via the extensive Indian Ocean networks.
Which of these was an official language of the Sultanate of Zanzibar?
Sultanate of Zanzibar: Swahili. It was also involved in the shortest war in history, the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted 38 minutes on the morning of 27 August 1896.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria?
Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria: German. It maintained a degree of provincial autonomy, and its status remained unchanged until the dissolution of the monarchy in 1918.
Which of these was an official language of Denmark–Norway?
Denmark–Norway: Danish. The state also claimed sovereignty over three historical peoples: Frisians, Gutes and Wends.
Which country used the grivna as its official currency?
The grivna is the official currency of Novgorod Republic. For much of its history, Novgorod was the center of Russian art and culture.
This messianic movement arose in British India in the late 19th century after its founder declared himself the promised Messiah and Mahdi — what movement is it?
Ahmadiyya is an Islamic messianic movement originating in British India in the late 19th century.
The longest-serving Home Affairs Minister in Indian history, this politician also led the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party as its president from 2014 to 2020 — who is he?
Amit Shah (born 22 October 1964) is an Indian politician who has served as the 31st Minister of Home Affairs since 2019, the longest-serving holder of the office in Indian history.

This 19th-century Habsburg-Lorraine royal fathered two emperors — one who ruled from Vienna, the other who ruled Mexico — and was grandfather to the royal whose 1914 assassination triggered World War I — who is he?
Archduke Franz Karl of Austria (17 December 1802 - 8 March 1878) was a member of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine.
Fought in southern Anatolia on 5 November 333 BC, this clash saw Alexander the Great rout Darius III, who fled leaving behind his family and treasury — which engagement was it?
Battle of Issus (also Issos) occurred in southern Anatolia, on 5 November 333 BC between the Hellenic League led by Alexander the Great and the Achaemenid (or Persian) Empire, led by Darius III.
Widow of King Prasutagus, which queen of the Iceni tribe led a failed revolt against Roman occupation of Britain around AD 60?

An Argentine Marxist revolutionary whose stylized image became a countercultural icon of rebellion, he was horrified by poverty and inequality while traveling as a medical student. His involvement in Guatemala's social reforms led him to become a major figure of which revolution?
Che Guevara (14 June 1928 - 9 October 1967) was an Argentine Marxist revolutionary, author, guerrilla leader, diplomat, politician, and military theorist.
This Swedish diplomat became the youngest person ever elected UN Secretary-General at just 47, serving from 1953 until his death in a 1961 plane crash — who is he?

Dag Hammarskjöld (29 July 1905 - 18 September 1961) was a Swedish economist and diplomat who served as the second Secretary-General of the United Nations from April 1953 until his death in a plane crash in September 1961.
Nominated three times for the Medal of Honor and finally awarded it for his WWII service in the Philippines, this American general also served as Army chief of staff in the 1930s. Who is he?
Douglas MacArthur (26 January 1880 - 5 April 1964) was an American general who served as a top commander during World War II and the Korean War, achieving the rank of General of the Army.

A World War I officer decorated with the Pour le Mérite, he later wrote the tactics classic 'Infantry Attacks' and commanded the 7th Panzer Division — though history remembers him as 'The Desert Fox.' Who was he?
Erwin Rommel (15 November 1891 - 14 October 1944), known as The Desert Fox, was a German Generalfeldmarschall (field marshal) during World War II.
This Norse goddess of love, beauty, and war owns a magical necklace called Brísingamen, rides a chariot pulled by two cats, and can transform into a falcon using an enchanted cloak — who is she?
Freyja (Old Norse '(the) Lady') is a goddess associated with love, beauty, fertility, sex, war, gold, and seir (magic for seeing and influencing the future).
Founded in 918, this Korean kingdom achieved what historians call the peninsula's first true national unification, ruling until the Joseon dynasty was established in 1392 — what kingdom was it?

Goryeo (Middle) was a Korean state founded in 918, during a time of national division called the Later Three Kingdoms period, that unified and ruled the Korean Peninsula until the establishment of Joseon in 1392.
Often depicted holding twin torches or a key, or accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, magic, and witchcraft first appeared in Hesiod's Theogony in the 8th century BCE — who is she?

Hecate (Ancient) is a goddess in ancient Greek religion and mythology, most often shown holding a pair of torches, a key, or snakes, or accompanied by dogs, and in later periods depicted as three-formed or triple-bodied.

Descended from a Welsh noble family and Catherine of Valois, this English and Welsh royal dynasty held the throne from 1485 to 1603 across five monarchs including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I — name the dynasty?
House of Tudor was an English and Welsh dynasty that held the throne of England from 1485 to 1603.
This Israeli far-right politician has served as minister of national security since 2022 and leads a Kahanist party called 'Jewish Power.' Who is he?
Itamar Ben-Gvir (born 6 May 1976) is an Israeli politician and lawyer who has served as the minister of national security since 2022, except for a two-month gap in early 2025.
This California politician served two non-consecutive stints as governor decades apart, making him both the state's oldest and, at the time, its sixth-youngest governor — who is he?
Jerry Brown (born April 7, 1938) is an American lawyer, author, and politician who served as the 34th and 39th governor of California from 1975 to 1983 and 2011 to 2019.
Overthrown in 1955 yet returned to Argentina's presidency in 1973, this military-college graduate gave his name to a political force still shaping the country — who?

Juan Perón (8 October 1895 - 1 July 1974) was an Argentine military officer and politician who was the 29th and 40th president of Argentina, serving from 1946 to his overthrow in 1955, and from 1973 until his death in 1974.

Founded around 1000 AD when Stephen I was crowned its first king, this Central European monarchy — later split by Ottoman occupation into three parts — endured for nearly a millennium until 1946. What was it?
Kingdom of Hungary was a monarchy in Central Europe that existed for nearly a millennium, from 1000 to 1946.

This US Army officer served with the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne during World War II, and was portrayed by Ron Livingston in the HBO miniseries Band of Brothers — who is he?

Lewis Nixon III (September 30, 1918 - January 11, 1995) was a United States Army officer who, during World War II, served at the company, battalion, and regimental level with the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division.

Quoted by Jesus in 'You cannot serve both God and ___,' this New Testament word for wealth was later personified in medieval tradition as one of the seven princes of Hell, representing greed — what's the word?
Mammon is commonly thought to mean money, material wealth, or any entity that promises wealth, and is associated with the greedy pursuit of gain.
This American memoirist and poet's first of seven autobiographies, published in 1969, told of her life up to age 17 and brought her international recognition. Who is she?
Maya Angelou (born Marguerite Annie Johnson; April 4, 1928 - May 28, 2014) was an American memoirist, essayist, poet, and civil rights activist.
Known as "The Proclamator," this independence activist was once jailed in the Boven Digoel concentration camp before becoming his country's very first vice president. Who was he?

Mohammad Hatta (n Athar; 12 August 1902 - 14 March 1980) was an Indonesian statesman, nationalist, and independence activist who served as the country's first vice president as well as the third prime minister.

Most often used as an insult and rarely pinned to one clear definition, this late-20th-century ideology champions free-market capitalism through lower taxes, privatization and deregulation — what is it called?
Neoliberalism is a political and economic ideology that advocates for free-market capitalism, which became dominant in policy-making from the late 20th century onward.
According to Genesis, this second son of Judah defied the custom of levirate marriage with his brother Er's widow, Tamar, and was punished for it — who was he?
Onan was a figure detailed in the Book of Genesis chapter 38, as the second son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shuah.
This Confucian scholar-turned-revolutionary led rebel armies against French colonial forces in 19th-century Vietnam, refusing to surrender even after they desecrated his ancestral tombs. Who was he?
Phan Đình Phùng (1847 - January 21, 1896) was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led rebel armies against French colonial forces in Vietnam.
Born in 1988, this Indian politician served as an MLA from Delhi's Rajinder Nagar before joining the Rajya Sabha in 2022 and later switching parties to the BJP — who is he?
Raghav Chadha (born 11 November 1988) is an Indian politician and chartered accountant who serves as a Member of Parliament in the Rajya Sabha since 2022.

Rising to major general by 1979, this South Korean army officer backed his military academy friend's coup that year and later became, in 1987, the first president chosen by direct popular vote. Who is he?
Roh Tae-woo (4 December 1932 - 26 October 2021) was a South Korean army general and politician who served as the sixth president of South Korea from 1988 to 1993.

This Indian politician served as governor of five different states — including Jammu and Kashmir — after earlier representing Aligarh in the national parliament as a member of the Janata Dal. Who is he?

Satya Pal Malik (24 July 1946 - 5 August 2025) was an Indian politician, lawyer and statesman who served as governor of five Indian states, namely Bihar, Odisha, Jammu and Kashmir, Goa, and Meghalaya.
Educated in the United States before marrying revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen in 1915, she was later named Honorary Chairman of the People's Republic just before her death in 1981 — who was she?
Soong Ching-ling (27 January 1893 - 29 May 1981; Christian name Rosamonde or Rosamond) was a Chinese politician.
Under this Roman power-sharing system, the roles of augustus and caesar were likened to Jupiter and his son Hercules, and it endured from 293 to 324 — what was it called?

Tetrarchy was the system instituted by Roman emperor Diocletian to govern the ancient Roman Empire by dividing it between two emperors, the augusti, and their junior colleagues and designated successors, the caesares.

This German admiral led the Abwehr military intelligence service from 1935 to 1944, and despite initially supporting Hitler, turned to acts of resistance against the Nazi regime after the invasion of Poland — who was he?
Wilhelm Canaris (1 January 1887 - 9 April 1945) was a German admiral and the chief of the Abwehr (the German military-intelligence service) from 1935 to 1944.

A close associate of Mahatma Gandhi and a founding member of the Jamia Millia Islamia university, this Hyderabad-born educationist rose to serve as president of India from 1967 until his death two years later — who was he?

Zakir Husain (8 February 1897 - 3 May 1969) was an Indian educationist and politician who served as the vice president of India from 1962 to 1967 and president of India from 13 May 1967 until his death on 3 May 1969.

Captured as a child and given as a gift to Peter the Great, this military engineer of African origin rose through the Russian imperial court and became an ancestor of poet Alexander Pushkin — who is he?
Abram Petrovich Gannibal: African-born Russian general and military engineer.
Son of a Tennessee senator, he sat as vice president for eight years before narrowly losing the 2000 presidential race to George W. Bush. Which environmentalist and Democrat is it?
Al Gore: Vice President of the United States from 1993 to 2001.
Succeeding his father Omar to extend Gabon's first political dynasty, this president ruled from 2009 until a 2023 coup deposed him — who is he?
Ali Bongo: President of Gabon from 2009 to 2023. A member of the Gabonese Democratic Party, Bongo is the son of Omar Bongo, who was president from 1967 until his death in 2009.
The son of a former Kentucky governor, this Democrat has served as governor of the state since 2019 and is eyeing a 2028 presidential run — who is he?
Andy Beshear: Governor of Kentucky since 2019. Andrew Graham Beshear ( bə-SHEER; born November 29, 1977) is an American politician and attorney serving since 2019 as the 63rd governor of Kentucky.
Trained as a barrister in London before leading a Hyderabad-based Indian political party founded by his family, who is this five-term MP repeatedly named among the world's most influential Muslims?

Born in Honolulu, this Harvard Law graduate became the first African American president of the Harvard Law Review before serving as a U.S. Senator and eventually leading the nation from 2009 to 2017. Who is he?
Barack Obama: President of the United States from 2009 to 2017.
A French businessman who owned both Adidas and the football club Olympique de Marseille, he also dabbled as an actor, singer and even Minister of the City. Who is he?
Bernard Tapie: French businessman and politician (1943–2021)
This 19th-century religious leader served as the second president of a major American church and doubled as the first governor of Utah Territory. Who is he?

This ancient state, whose territory mostly overlapped modern Azerbaijan, gets its Western name from a Greek mistranslation of an Armenian term — which historical realm is this, whose descendants include the Udi people?

Caucasian Albania: Ancient state in the Caucasus. Caucasian Albania is a modern exonym for a former state located in ancient times in the Caucasus, mostly overlapping the region of present-day Azerbaijan.
Mentally ill for most of his reign, this 18th-century Danish-Norwegian king let his court physician rule as a de facto dictator from 1770 to 1772 before a coup deposed the doctor — who was the king?
Christian VII: King of Denmark and Norway from 1766 to 1808.
Elected to Newark's council after a 10-day hunger strike in a tent, this Rhodes Scholar became the city's 38th mayor before becoming New Jersey's first African-American U.S. senator — who is he?

The longest-serving prime minister of Iceland and former mayor of Reykjavík, he later chaired the Central Bank — and the 2008 financial crisis sparked loud public demands for his resignation. Who was he?
This Polish historian-turned-politician led the European Council from 2014 to 2019 before returning home to become his country's longest-serving post-communist prime minister — who is he?
Donald Tusk: Prime Minister of Poland (2007–2014; since 2023)
Elected to Israel's Knesset at just 28, this politician later served two terms as Mayor of Jerusalem before becoming prime minister from 2006 to 2009 — who is he?
Ehud Olmert: Prime Minister of Israel from 2006 to 2009. The son of a former Herut politician, Olmert was first elected to the Knesset for Likud in 1973, at the age of 28.
Leading the Communist Party of Germany from 1925 to 1933, this revolutionary sought to overthrow the Weimar Republic and branded rival Social Democrats as 'social fascists' — who is he?
The son of a wealthy Spanish farmer, this Cuban revolutionary picked up anti-imperialist ideas studying law in Havana before ruling the island from 1959 to 2008 — who was he?
Fidel Castro: Leader of Cuba from 1959 to 2008.
Governing France from the fall of Napoleon III in 1870 until the Nazi invasion of 1940, this parliamentary system weathered the Paris Commune and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine — what was it?

French Third Republic: Government of France from 1870 to 1940. Consequently, the Third Republic, originally envisioned as a provisional government, instead became the permanent form of government of France.

A physician turned journalist, this French prime minister demanded total victory after 1.4 million of his countrymen died in the First World War and pushed through the Treaty of Versailles's harsh terms. Who was he?
Georges Clemenceau: Prime Minister of France (1906–1909, 1917–1920)

A trained physician, this politician became Norway's first female prime minister in 1981, later led the World Health Organization, and chaired the UN commission that popularized the term 'sustainable development.' Who is she?

Son of a Memphis congressman who held the same House seat for 22 years, this Tennessee Democrat represented the same district before an unsuccessful 2006 Senate bid and later became a Morgan Stanley executive — who is he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
This high-ranking Nazi SS officer served as Hitler's liaison to Heinrich Himmler and became the Führer's brother-in-law-by-marriage through his wedding to Eva Braun's sister. Who is he?
Hermann Fegelein: German Nazi Waffen-SS commander (1906–1945)
Born Su Zhu, he succeeded Mao Zedong as China's top leader in the 1970s before being gradually eased out of power between 1978 and 1981 — who is he?
Hua Guofeng: Leader of China from 1976 to 1978.

Promoted by the Discovery Institute and resting on claims of 'irreducible complexity' and 'specified complexity,' this pseudoscientific argument for a designer was rebutted by scientific scrutiny — what is it?
Intelligent design: Pseudoscientific argument for the existence of God.
Only the second democratically elected president of Guatemala, this army officer's sweeping 1950s land-reform program rippled across Latin America before he was toppled — who was he?
Jacobo Árbenz: President of Guatemala from 1951 to 1954.
Hailed as the architect of Britain's conquest of New France in the Seven Years' War, this field marshal became the first British governor general of what became Canada — who was he?
Jeffery Amherst, 1st Baron Amherst: British Army general (1717–1797)

Developing the theory of 'offensive realism' at the University of Chicago, this political scientist argued in a 2007 book that a pro-Israel lobby wields outsized influence over American foreign policy — who is he?
As founder of the antisemitic newspaper Der Stürmer and Gauleiter of Franconia, this Nazi propagandist became the first member of the regime convicted of inciting genocide at Nuremberg — who was he?
Julius Streicher: German publicist and politician (1885–1946)
Imprisoned for a decade on Robben Island for anti-apartheid activism, this South African later stepped in as president after Thabo Mbeki resigned — who was he?
Kgalema Motlanthe: President of South Africa from 2008 to 2009.
Grandson of the Mongol Empire's founder, this ruler proclaimed the dynastic name 'Great Yuan' in 1271 and became the first emperor of a new Chinese dynasty — who was he?
Kublai Khan: Emperor of Yuan China from 1271 to 1294.

A founder of the Israeli Labor Party, this prime minister succeeded Ben-Gurion in 1963, ended military rule over Israeli Arab citizens, and became the first Israeli leader formally invited to the White House — who is he?
Levi Eshkol: Prime Minister of Israel from 1963 to 1969.

This Colombian liberal politician and journalist, who founded the New Liberalism movement and declared himself an enemy of the drug cartels, was assassinated in 1989 before the presidential vote — who was he?

Luis Carlos Galán: Colombian politician (1943–1989). While the investigation into his assassination remains unsolved, Galan's assassination was a crucial factor in the downfall of the Medellin Cartel a few years later.
Sanskrit for 'circle,' this geometric configuration of symbols is used across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Shinto traditions to aid meditation and represent sacred space — what is it?
Mandala: Spiritual and ritual symbol in Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism.
Famed for slicing his military cloak in two with his sword to clothe a freezing beggar, this Roman-cavalry-veteran-turned-bishop became one of Europe's most venerated patron saints — who was he?
Martin of Tours: Christian cleric and saint (316/336–397)
Originating in Judaism, this Hebrew term for an anointed savior figure describes a future human leader descended from King David who will reunite the tribes of Israel — what is the title?
Messiah: Saviour or liberator of a group of people.

Historians generally date this current period of human history from around 1500, though many now reserve its label for events from the 19th century onward, like the Industrial Revolution — what span of time is this?
Modern era: Current period of history. Since the 1990s, it has been more common among historians to refer to the period after the Middle Ages and up to the 19th century as the early modern period.
Born in 1664, which Ottoman sultan ruled the empire from 1695 until his death in 1703?

Mustafa II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1695 to 1703. Mustafa II (Ottoman Turkish: مصطفى ثانى Muṣṭafā-yi sānī; 6 February 1664 – 29 December 1703) was the sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1695 to 1703.
Mentioned only in John's Gospel among the New Testament writers, this Pharisee and Sanhedrin member secretly admired Jesus and earned the nickname 'defender of Jesus' — who is he?
Nicodemus: Pharisee, biblical figure appearing in the Gospel of John.
Elected as Toronto's mayor in 2023, this former NDP member of Parliament was previously married to a fellow NDP leader who led the Official Opposition in 2011 — who is she?
Serving as Speaker pro tempore for 22 days after Kevin McCarthy's removal, this North Carolina Republican chaired the House Financial Services Committee from 2023 to 2025 — who is he?
Known from early medieval carved stones, this people lived north of the Firth of Forth before merging with Dál Riata to form the Kingdom of Alba — who were they?
Picts: Medieval tribal confederation in northern Britain.
Educated at Sandhurst in England, this man returned home in 1966 and ruled for nearly half a century, becoming the longest-serving leader in the Arab world at his death — which sultan?
Qaboos bin Said: Sultan of Oman from 1970 to 2020.
Historians use this name for the wave of anticlerical violence — killings and church arson — carried out by leftist groups during the Spanish Civil War; what's it called?
Golden age of arcade video games
Red Terror (Spain): Assassinations during the Spanish Civil War.
As Colombia's Minister of Justice, he cracked down on cocaine traffickers until he was assassinated on the orders of a notorious drug baron in 1984 — who was he?
Rodrigo Lara Bonilla: Colombian lawyer and politician (1946-1984)
Born into the Dinka and a rebel fighter from the age of 15, he became the first president of the world's newest nation when it gained independence in July 2011 — who is he?
Salva Kiir: President of South Sudan since 2011.
A member of Japan's Liberal Democratic Party, this politician served as Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary and State Minister for Foreign Affairs under the Third Abe Cabinet — who is he?
Discovered hiding in Guam's jungle in 1972, this Japanese army sergeant was one of the last WWII holdouts found nearly three decades after the fighting ended — who was he?
Shoichi Yokoi: Japanese World War II holdout (1915–1997)
This mythical creature combines a human head with a lion's body — in Greek myth she poses a fatal riddle to Oedipus, while in Egyptian tradition it's an unwinged, benevolent guardian — what is it?

Sphinx: Mythological creature with a human head and lion body. In Greek tradition, the sphinx is a treacherous and merciless being with the head of a woman, the haunches of a lion, and the wings of a bird.
In 2007 this French politician became the first woman to reach the second round of a presidential election, ultimately losing to Nicolas Sarkozy — who is she?
Raised by his mother Aethra before discovering his royal father in Athens, this Greek hero is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus: Legendary king of Athens who slayed the Minotaur.
Founded by Mamata Banerjee in 1998 as a breakaway faction, this West Bengal party ruled from 2011 until finally losing to the BJP in the 2026 election — which party?
Trinamool Congress: Political party in India.
The last man standing in the Year of the Four Emperors, this Roman founded the Flavian dynasty and was the first emperor to rise from an equestrian family. Who was he?
Vespasian: Roman emperor from AD 69 to 79.

Fought alongside a wider Georgian civil conflict, this early-1990s fight pitted government forces against separatists backed by North Caucasian militants, Cossacks, and the Russian military — which conflict?
War in Abkhazia (1992–1993): Conflict between Georgia and Abkhaz separatists.

A German Army intelligence officer in occupied Warsaw during WWII, this man is credited with saving several Polish Jews, including pianist Władysław Szpilman — his story was dramatized in The Pianist. Who was he?
Wilm Hosenfeld: German army officer (1895–1952) and Righteous among the Nations.

After helping secure the Qing dynasty's abdication, this Chinese general became the Republic's first formal president, only to declare himself emperor in 1915 and abdicate again months later — who was he?
Yuan Shikai: First president of the Republic of China (1859–1916)
Which one below was born first?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was born earliest?

Ivan Pavlov (born 1849) is the earliest of the four. Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Pope Sylvester II is an astronomer.
Which of these is a mathematician?
Grigori Perelman is a mathematician. The full details of Perelman's work were filled in and explained by various authors over the following several years.
What is the atomic number of Rutherfordium?
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rf and atomic number 104.
What is the atomic number of Selenium?
Selenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Se and atomic number 34.
In what year did B. R. Ambedkar die?
B. R. Ambedkar: Ambedkar served as Law and Justice minister in the first cabinet of Jawaharlal Nehru.
In what year was Hydrogen discovered?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Mil Mi-8: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mi-8 is the world's most-produced helicopter, with over 17,000 units used by over 50 countries.
Semen: prostate. Semen, also known as seminal fluid, is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.
Who is credited with discovering Niobium?
Niobium: Charles Hatchett. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Who is credited with discovering Peroxisome?
Peroxisome: Christian de Duve. A peroxisome is a membrane-bound organelle, a type of microbody, found in the cytoplasm of virtually all eukaryotic cells.
Who is credited with discovering Uncertainty principle?
Uncertainty principle: Werner Heisenberg. The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.
Who is credited with discovering Mensa?
Mensa (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for table, though it originally commemorated Table Mountain and was known as "Mons Mensae".

The first woman to officially attend a Dutch university, she became one of the Netherlands' earliest female physicians and, in 1882, opened the world's first birth control clinic — who was this suffrage leader?
Aletta Jacobs (Dutch; 9 February 1854 - 10 August 1929) was a Dutch physician and women's suffrage activist.
Multicellular, oxygen-breathing, and all descended from a single common ancestor, this kingdom ranges in size from 8.5 micrometers to 33.6 meters. What is it?
Animal are multicellular, eukaryotic organisms belonging to the biological kingdom Animalia.

This German philosopher's 1818 masterwork describes the visible world as the manifestation of a blind, irrational underlying will, building on Kantian idealism while rejecting German idealism's optimism — who is he?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 - 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.
Belonging to the Colubridae family of venomous snakes and found only in Sub-Saharan Africa, this reptile's scientific name is Dispholidus typus — what is it commonly called?
Boomslang (or; Dispholidus typus) is a highly venomous snake in the family Colubridae.

Native to tropical Africa, this vine's fruit can be eaten young as a vegetable, or left to mature, dry out, and be hollowed into a ladle, bowl, drinking vessel, or musical instrument — name this plant?

Calabash (Lagenaria siceraria), also known as bottle gourd, white-flowered gourd, long melon, birdhouse gourd, New Guinea bean, New Guinea butter bean, Tasmania bean, zucca melon and opo squash, is a vine which is grown for its fruit.
Separated from the small intestine by the ileocecal valve, this pouch — whose Latin root means 'blind' — kicks off the large intestine and, in herbivores, helps ferment cellulose. What is it?
Cecum (plural ceca or) is a pouch within the peritoneum that is considered to be the beginning of the large intestine.

An organic compound found naturally in citrus fruits with the formula C6H8O7, over two million tons are manufactured annually for use as an acidifier, flavoring, and preservative. What is this compound?
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7. In biochemistry, it is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, which occurs in the metabolism of all aerobic organisms.

What zoological term describes the internal-fertilization mating behavior in which a male animal introduces sperm directly into a female's reproductive tract — occurring via a 'cloacal kiss' in birds and most reptiles, or vaginally in mammals?
Copulation (zoology) is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
What unit of time, roughly 24 hours long, marks one full rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun and drives the circadian rhythms of most living things?
Day is the time period of a full rotation of the Earth with respect to the Sun.
This C-shaped first section of the small intestine connects the stomach to the jejunum and is the body's principal site for absorbing iron — what is it?
Duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
Built from flattened cells atop a columnar basal layer, this outer skin barrier regulates water loss and grows thinner as a person ages — what is it?
Epidermis is the outermost of the three major layers that constitute the skin, the inner layers being the dermis and hypodermis.

Named for a physicist who reportedly asked 'But where is everybody?' over lunch in 1950, this puzzle contrasts the vast odds of alien civilizations with our total lack of evidence for them — what's it called?
Fermi paradox is the term for the apparent gap between the lack of conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the apparently high likelihood of their existence.
Caused by a loss of blood supply, this type of tissue death most commonly affects the feet and hands and can turn skin red or black. What condition is it?
Gangrene is a type of tissue death caused by a lack of blood supply. If the gangrene is caused by an infectious agent, it may present with a fever or sepsis.
Defined as one joule of absorbed radiation energy per kilogram of matter, this SI measure is used in radiotherapy dosing and predicting acute radiation sickness — which measure is this?
Gray (unit) (symbol: Gy) is the unit of ionizing radiation dose in the International System of Units (SI), defined as the absorption of one joule of radiation energy per kilogram of matter.
Classified as acute if it resolves within six months and chronic if it persists longer, this inflammation of the liver can progress to cirrhosis or liver cancer — which condition?
Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver tissue. Acute hepatitis can resolve on its own, progress to chronic hepatitis, or (rarely) result in acute liver failure.

This altered mental state involves intensely focused attention, reduced awareness of surroundings, and heightened responsiveness to suggestion, though scientists still debate whether it's truly a distinct state of consciousness — what is it?

Hypnosis is a human condition involving focused attention (the selective attention/selective inattention hypothesis, SASI), reduced peripheral awareness, and an enhanced capacity to respond to suggestion.
Eaten raw or turned into jams and wine, this round Brazilian fruit is famous for growing directly on the trunk of its own tree — what is it?
Jabuticaba is a round, edible fruit produced by a jaboticaba tree (Plinia cauliflora), also known as Brazilian grapetree.
This Columbia economist won the Nobel in 2001 and famously skewers his laissez-faire colleagues as "free-market fundamentalists" — who is he?
Joseph Stiglitz (born February 9, 1943) is an American New Keynesian economist, a public policy analyst, political activist, and a professor at Columbia University.
What reddish-brown, alcohol-based tincture of opium, roughly 10% opium by weight, was historically sold without a prescription as a pain reliever and cough suppressant until the early 20th century?
Laudanum is a tincture of opium containing approximately 10% powdered opium by weight (the equivalent of 1% morphine).
Because its large profile and low operating altitude make it an easy target, this heavily armed gunship variant of the C-130 Hercules usually flies missions at night. What aircraft is it?
Lockheed AC-130 is a heavily armed, long-endurance, ground-attack variant of the C-130 Hercules transport, fixed-wing aircraft.

One of the most colorful mammals alive, this west-central African monkey wears red and blue on both its face and its rump, with the brightest males being the biggest — long mistaken for a baboon, what is it?
Mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx) is a large Old World monkey native to west central Africa.

Sold in Europe as part of a blended sedative called Mandrax alongside an antihistamine, this sedative-hypnotic drug of the quinazolinone class was pulled from many markets in the 1980s due to widespread misuse — name this compound?
Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic medication that was widely prescribed during the mid-20th century.

Sharing the insect order Lepidoptera with butterflies but typically sporting duller, darker wing patterns, this group includes roughly 160,000 mostly nocturnal species, many still undescribed by science — name this group of insects?
Moth are a group of winged insect of the order Lepidoptera, the other well-known members of which are butterflies, they are characterized by dark or dull patterned wings.
Found in tobacco and trace amounts of tomatoes and eggplants, this nightshade alkaloid is used recreationally as a stimulant yet acts as a deadly neurotoxin to insects — what is it?
Nicotine is an alkaloid found primarily in plants of the nightshade family, notably in tobacco; it is also synthesized.

Sitting in life's hierarchy between tissue and a full body system, this term describes a group of different tissues — like the epithelial and muscle layers of the gut wall — joined to serve one shared function. What is it?
Organ (biology) is a collection of tissues joined in a structural unit to serve a common function.

The males of this Phasianidae bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic species include blue, green, and a third found only in the Congo Basin — what is this bird, collectively?

Peafowl is a common name for two bird species of the genus Pavo and one species of the closely related genus Afropavo within the tribe Pavonini of the family Phasianidae (the pheasants and their allies).

Enclosed in a papery husk formed from its calyx, the fruit of this nightshade-family genus tastes like a firm tomato crossed with a sweet, tangy grape — nearly half of its species grow only in Mexico. Name the genus?
Physalis (from Ancient) is a genus of approximately 75 to 90 flowering plants in the nightshade family (Solanaceae), which are native to the Americas and Australasia.
Element number 19, this silvery alkali metal reacts so eagerly with air that it forms flaky white peroxide within seconds — and its symbol K comes from the Neo-Latin word kalium. What is it?
Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
This collective name covers several genera of mid-sized game birds, split between Old World and New World families despite their similar appearance — what birds are they?
Quail is a collective name for several genera of mid-sized birds generally placed in the order Galliformes.

Winner of the 1905 Nobel Prize for his work on tuberculosis, this German physician identified the causative agents of tuberculosis, cholera, and anthrax, earning him the nickname 'father of microbiology' alongside Louis Pasteur — name this scientist?
Robert Koch (KOKH; 11 December 1843 - 27 May 1910) was a German physician and microbiologist.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes patches of thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers in cold weather, with one severe subtype called CREST syndrome — what condition is it?
Scleroderma is a group of autoimmune diseases that may result in changes to the skin, blood vessels, muscles, and internal organs.
This structural framework supporting an animal's body comes in three main forms — a rigid outer shell, a rigid inner frame, or a flexible fluid-supported structure — what is it called?
Skeleton is the structural frame that supports the body of most animals.

Described as the most extreme form of malnutrition, this severe shortfall of caloric energy is so grave that deliberately inflicting it on a population is a crime under international law — what is it?
Starvation is a severe deficiency in caloric energy intake, below the level needed to maintain an organism's life.

Restricted today to Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines, these tree-dwelling primates make up the only living family in their taxonomic order and thrive in liana-rich forests — which animal?
Tarsier are haplorhine primates of the family Tarsiidae, which is the lone extant family within the infraorder Tarsiiformes.
Found in nature only as an oxide and locked in minerals like rutile and ilmenite, this strong, silvery element bears the name of mythological giants — what is it?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Native to cool climates across the Northern Hemisphere, this low shrub bears small, round, edible fruit of a deep blue color, and goes by several folk names depending on region — what's the species?
Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, and whortleberry.
This American child prodigy, son of a prominent psychiatrist, lectured on four-dimensional geometry at age 12 and graduated from Harvard cum laude at 16. Who was he?

William James Sidis (April 1, 1898 - July 17, 1944) was an American child prodigy whose exceptional abilities in mathematics and languages made him one of the most famous intellectual prodigies of the early 20th century.
This American psychologist devised a pyramid-shaped theory of human needs culminating in self-actualization, and was later ranked the 10th most-cited psychologist of the 20th century — who is he?

First flown as a stretched derivative of a popular narrow-body jet family in 1994, this twin-engine airliner carries up to 239 passengers and later gained a fuel-efficient 'neo' version with new winglets — which aircraft?
Airbus A321: Airliner, stretched model of the A320 family.
Native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa, this flowering plant lent its name — and originally its root — to a fluffy campfire treat, and is used in herbal medicine — which plant?
Triggered by either histamine or bradykinin, this rapid swelling of the deep skin layers can affect the face, tongue, or airway within minutes — what is it?
Angioedema: Disease characterized by rapid swelling.

Studying humanity's past through the recovery of artifacts and sites — including stone tools dating back 3.3 million years — this discipline sits at the crossroads of the social sciences and humanities — which field?
Archaeology: Study of human activity based on materials left behind.

This rapid, irregular quivering of the heart's upper chambers can be entirely silent or bring palpitations and fainting — and it sharply raises the risk of stroke, dementia and heart failure. What is this arrhythmia?
Atrial fibrillation: Irregular beating of the atria of the heart.
First flown in 1947 with a distinctive V-tail, this single-engine aircraft holds the record for the longest continuous production run in aviation history — which model?
Beechcraft Bonanza: Family of single engine American light aircraft, first flown in 1945.

Despite its name, this snake is actually grey to dark brown — the name instead describes the dark interior of its mouth, displayed as a threat — which species, the second-longest venomous snake after the king cobra?
Black mamba: Species of venomous snake. The black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis) is a species of highly venomous snake belonging to the family Elapidae.
This subfamily of horned, cloven-hooved ungulates includes cattle, bison, and both African and water buffalo, with the gaur as its largest living member — which group?
Jointly developed by Pakistan and China as a lightweight fourth-generation fighter meant to eventually succeed the F-16 in Pakistan's air force, this jet's Chinese designation is FC-1 — what is it?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Sino-Pakistani multirole fighter aircraft.
This medical emergency occurs when the heart suddenly stops beating effectively, cutting off blood flow to the brain and other organs within minutes — what is it called?
Cardiac arrest: Sudden or unexpected loss of heartbeat.
Latin for 'little brain,' this hindbrain structure fine-tunes motor coordination and timing without actually initiating movement — what is it?
Cerebellum: Structure at the rear of the vertebrate brain, beneath the cerebrum.

Caused by a bacterium spread through contaminated water and undercooked shellfish, this intestinal infection produces severe watery diarrhea that can trigger dehydration within hours — which disease is it?
Cholera: Bacterial infection of the small intestine.
Recognizable by a prominent crest and curved bill, this Australasian parrot family includes 21 species, the smallest of which is the cockatiel — which family of birds?
Cockatoo: Any bird in the family Cacatuidae.
These colonial marine invertebrates secrete calcium carbonate to build the hard skeletons that form tropical reefs — what are they?
Coral: Marine invertebrates of the subphylum Anthozoa.
Once sold under the brand name Flexeril and chemically similar to tricyclic antidepressants, this oral medication treats sudden muscle spasms — what's the drug?
Cyclobenzaprine: Muscle relaxant medication. It should not be used together with MAOIs.
Whether for an object, a process, or a system, this is the intentional concept or proposal created by a thinking agent, balancing purpose, aesthetics, and constraints — what single word names it?
Design: Plan for the construction of an object or system.
Despite its common names, this evergreen conifer isn't a true member of the pine, spruce, or hemlock genera, yet stands as the tallest species in its own family — what is it?
Douglas fir: Species of tree. It is native to western North America and is also known as Douglas-fir, Douglas spruce, Oregon pine, and Columbian pine.
This unit of energy equals the kinetic energy a single electron gains while crossing an electric potential difference of one volt — what is it called?
Sometimes abbreviated ETM, this antibiotic treats everything from respiratory infections to syphilis and is the eye ointment routinely dabbed on newborns to prevent eye infections. What is it?
Erythromycin: Antibiotic medication. Erythromycin (sometimes abbreviated ETM in reports) is an antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
Native to the Iberian Peninsula and introduced to hundreds of locations worldwide, this grassland herbivore digs extensive burrow networks called warrens — what is it?
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
A French economist who gave up accounting to lecture across France, he founded peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union before sharing the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. Who was he?
Frédéric Passy: French economist and pacifist (1822–1912)
Ranging from Baja California to Japan's coast, this cephalopod is the largest of its kind on Earth and a common aquarium favorite — which creature?
Giant Pacific octopus: Species of cephalopod. It can be found from the intertidal zone down to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), and is best-adapted to colder, oxygen- and nutrient-rich waters.
The seeds of five plants in this family, including rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane, cover 46% of the world's farmland — what group of plants is this?
Grass: Collective name for three families of plants.

This prehensile, multi-fingered body part sits at the end of primates' forelimbs — koalas famously have two opposable thumbs on each one, while raccoons are often said to have them despite lacking true opposable thumbs. What is it?
Hand: Extremity at the end of an arm or forelimb.

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Lightest and most abundant element in the universe, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter and fuels the stars — colorless, odorless, and highly combustible. What element is it?
Hydrogen: Chemical element with atomic number 1 (H)

Also known as the spectacled or binocellate snake, this reptile from South Asia is one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebites in the region and is revered in Hindu mythology — which snake?
Indian cobra: Species of snake. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.
Awarded a gas-attack Iron Cross in WWI before sharing the 1925 Nobel with Gustav Hertz for the laws of how an electron strikes an atom — who was this German-American physicist?
Hailed as a 'miracle worker' in 1955, this researcher refused to patent his polio vaccine so it could spread worldwide for free — who is he?
Jonas Salk: American inventor of the polio vaccine (1914–1995)
Made from shredded pastry dough layered with cheese and soaked in sugar syrup, this Arab dessert is especially popular during Ramadan, with a famous variant hailing from Nablus — what is it?

One of the five big cats in the genus Panthera, this slender, muscular predator wears dark spots clustered into rosettes and is split today into eight recognised subspecies across Africa and Asia — what is it?
Leopard: Species of cat native to Africa and Asia.

This American stealth strike fighter comes in three flavors — conventional, short-takeoff/vertical-landing, and carrier-based — and with 883 in service is the world's fourth-most-numerous military aircraft. What is it?

Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II: American stealth multirole fighter aircraft. The Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is an American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters.
With the formula MgCl2, this colorless salt forms hydrates and serves as the principal precursor to large-scale production of its namesake metal — what is it?
Magnesium chloride: Inorganic salt: MgCl2 and its hydrates. It forms hydrates MgCl2·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 12.
Widely brewed as a calming herbal tea despite limited clinical evidence for its effects, this annual plant in the daisy family goes by the nickname 'scented mayweed' — which plant?
Matricaria chamomilla: Species of flowering plant.
First isolated in 1921 and encoded by the codon AUG, this essential amino acid also serves as the precursor to cysteine — which amino acid is this?
Following the S phase and ending in cytokinesis, this equational cell division splits replicated chromosomes into two genetically identical daughter nuclei — what is the process called?
Mitosis: Cell division into two identical cells. Mitosis is a part of the cell cycle in eukaryotic cells in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
Taking its name from the Latin for 'weasel,' this is the largest family in the suborder Caniformia — gathering otters, badgers, martens, and wolverines under one roof. What is it?
Described by Eric Kandel as the 'epic challenge' of biology, this multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system — what field is it?
Neuroscience: Scientific study of the nervous system.
Thriving in the cool, wet summers of Northwest Europe, this hardy cereal grass tolerates low-nutrient, acidic soil and is dominated globally by Canadian and Russian production?
This fluid-filled sac that forms within the ovary is usually harmless and often tied to ovulation, appearing as a follicular or corpus luteum type — what is it?
Ovarian cyst: Fluid-filled sac in the ovary. If the cyst either breaks open or causes twisting of the ovary, it may cause severe pain.
This Austrian theoretical physicist, who befriended Einstein in Prague in 1912 and later hosted him often in Leiden, lent his name to a theorem and key work on phase transitions — who was he?

Approved for medical use in the US back in 1959 and sold under the brand name Adipex-P, this appetite-suppressing stimulant is a substituted amphetamine used alongside diet and exercise to treat obesity — what is it?

There are exactly five of these convex regular polyhedra — tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron — named for the philosopher who linked them to the classical elements. What are they called?
Platonic solid: Any of the five regular polyhedra. In geometry, a Platonic solid is a convex, regular polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space.
This legal document spells out how a business collects, stores, and shares personal details like your address, financial records, or medical history — what is it called?
Privacy policy: Management of personal data across media.
Recognizable by its bold red-and-black pattern, this true bug is often confused with the unrelated cinnamon bug and forms large aggregations across Europe and Asia — which species is it?
Pyrrhocoris apterus: Species of true bug. The firebug, Pyrrhocoris apterus, is a common insect of the family Pyrrhocoridae.
Scholars call it an "essentially contested concept" with no agreed definition, but it broadly links humanity to the supernatural through behaviors, ethics, texts and sacred places — what is it?

Nicknamed the 'dark lady of DNA,' this X-ray crystallographer's crucial contributions to the discovery of DNA's structure went largely unrecognized in her lifetime — James Watson believed she'd have won a Nobel Prize had she lived. Who was she?
Also called Besnier–Boeck–Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition forms clusters of inflammatory cells called granulomata, often starting in the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis: Abnormal formation of clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomata)
A slender African cat with a tiny head and enormous ears, this golden, black-spotted hunter is the sole member of its genus and stands tall on remarkably long legs — which wild cat is it?
Known commonly as baking soda, this white crystalline compound with the formula NaHCO3 occurs naturally as the mineral nahcolite — what is its chemical name?
Sodium bicarbonate: Chemical compound. It is a salt composed of a sodium cation (Na+) and a bicarbonate anion (HCO−3).
A luminous ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, the closest example to Earth is the Sun — what celestial object is this?
Star: Large self-illuminated object in space.
Despite the naming confusion with true yams, this starchy tuberous root actually belongs to the morning glory family and hails from tropical Ecuador — which crop?
Sweet potato: Species of edible plant.
Famously nicknamed 'white ants,' these wood-munching eusocial insects are actually genetically closer to cockroaches than they are to true ants — what are they?
Termite: Social insects related to cockroaches.
He joined Apple in 1998 to run worldwide operations and stepped up to the top job in 2011 when Steve Jobs resigned — which executive now leads the company?
Estimated to date back to the end of the Jurassic period roughly 156 million years ago, this fungal genus includes several species of truffles prized as culinary delicacies — which genus?
Tuber (fungus): Genus of fungi. Tuber is a genus in the fungal family Tuberaceae, with estimated molecular dating to the end of the Jurassic period (156 Mya).
The primary flavor compound in the vanilla bean, this phenolic aldehyde is now more often made synthetically than extracted from the real pod — what is it?
Vanillin: Chemical compound. Vanillin is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.
Awarded the 1932 Nobel Prize 'for the creation of quantum mechanics,' this German physicist also led his country's wartime nuclear program — who was he?
Ukraine's first female prime minister, she co-led the Orange Revolution and later led the Batkivshchyna party while championing EU integration — who is she?
Yulia Tymoshenko: Prime Minister of Ukraine (2005, 2007–2010)
What is the chemical symbol for lead?
The symbol for lead is Pb. Lead is a chemical element with the symbol Pb and atomic number 82.
The symbol for moscovium is Mc. Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.

Brittany Murphy: Murphy was born in Atlanta; her parents, Angelo Bertolotti and Sharon Murphy, divorced when she was three years old.
In what year was Howard Hughes born?
Howard Hughes: Howard Robard Hughes Jr. (December 24, 1905 – April 5, 1976) was an American aviator, aerospace engineer, business magnate, film producer, and investor.
In what year was Aubrey Plaza born?
Aubrey Plaza: Aubrey Christina Plaza (born June 26, 1984) is an American actress, comedian, writer, and producer.

Sofía Vergara: Sofía Margarita Vergara Vergara (Spanish: [soˈfi.a βeɾˈɣaɾa]; born July 10, 1972) is a Colombian and American actress and television personality.
In what year was Robin Wright born?
Robin Wright: Robin Gayle Wright (born April 8, 1966) is an American actress, producer and director.
In what year was Meghan, Duchess of Sussex born?
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex: Meghan was born and raised in Los Angeles, California.
In what year was Jennifer Lopez born?
Jennifer Lopez: Jennifer Lynn Lopez (born July 24, 1969) is an American singer, songwriter, actress, dancer, and businesswoman.
In what year was Ben Affleck born?
Ben Affleck: Benjamin Géza Affleck (born August 15, 1972) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Reneé Rapp born?
Reneé Rapp: Reneé Jane Rapp (born January 10, 2000) is an American singer-songwriter and actress.
In what year did Kirk Douglas die?
Kirk Douglas (born Issur Danielovitch; December 9, 1916 – February 5, 2020) was an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year did Treat Williams die?
Treat Williams: Richard Treat Williams Jr. (December 1, 1951 – June 12, 2023) was an American actor, whose career on stage and in film and television spanned five decades.
In what year was The Princess Diaries first released?
The Princess Diaries is a 2001 American coming-of-age comedy film directed by Garry Marshall from a screenplay by Gina Wendkos.
In what year was Extraction 2 first released?
